Statement of the sister who reported her missing.
I don’t know. Defne didn’t tell me everything.

Friday evening. I have a key. Her ID and wallet were on the table. But her backpack wasn’t in the wardrobe, and nor was her winter coat. There’s a camera at the building entrance; the manager told me.
Did you go to her flat?
Thursday evening, around seven. She called. She was normal; we talked about our mother’s birthday, she’d bought a present. Two or three minutes.
Holds her phone in her palm, waking the screen now and then.
When did you last speak to Defne?

At first it was a weight off. Then it felt strange. Defne doesn’t write ‘I’m fine’; she doesn’t say things like ‘I’m fine’ anyway, she either sends a voice note or calls. And it says ‘don’t call’. Who’s ‘you’? Mum and me? Still, we waited a day. That message made us wait.
As she showed the message, her thumb paused on the screen for a moment.
How did you take the message at 23.41?
“My sister doesn’t text ‘I’m fine’. She never has.”
She was tense. She was working until late, and when I asked she’d say ‘Work’. Once she said, ‘I know something, Buse, something I shouldn’t know,’ then laughed it off.
How was Defne in the last few weeks?
Buse Yalın — interview
Kuzey Hat Yapı. Progress payments, invoices, payments. Her manager was Halil Bey; she talked about him a few times. Meticulous, she said.
Where did she work?

Statement of the employee whose company car was seen in Bağlarbaşı that night.
Me. Site work; I leave early in the morning. Nobody else uses it.
Who keeps the company car in the evenings?
I’m on site; I don’t know about that side of things.
From finance. We get the progress payment paperwork from her. Hello, goodbye. I heard she’s gone missing; I’m sorry.
Do you know Defne Yalın?
That evening I went home after work. I live in Ümraniye. I watched the match.
Folded his arms across his chest.
Where were you on Thursday evening?
“That evening I went home after work.”
Cem Akbulut — interview
Interview held after the car park record.
…All right, I was there. Halil Bey asked me to pick up some paperwork. A file, to be collected from someone. I waited, nobody came, I left. I didn’t say because I didn’t want to muddle things.
His eyes slid to the door for a moment.
You said you went home. Your car is in Bağlarbaşı at 22.14.
Yes. I was on my phone. Time went by.
Cut the answer short.
You sat in the car for an hour and a half?
Cem Akbulut — second interview
I don’t know. Halil Bey said, ‘I’ll call and tell you.’ He didn’t call. So I sat in the car.
What paperwork? From whom?
…There’s no face in the footage.
Looked at the record for a long time. Then turned his head away.
I already said my car was there.
The man in the dark coat who takes something from the bench at 22.02 and puts it back at 00.06.
Interview held after the seafront camera and the cell tower record.
I made it up. I didn’t want to give Halil Bey away, but I didn’t want to… myself either. I told you half of it, that’s all.
The paperwork story?

…I sent it. I took the phone, I sent the message, I put it back. There was no lock; I opened it, I looked. So her family would wait one night. Not to hurt anyone. I didn’t touch Defne, I swear; she got away anyway, we couldn’t find her.
Rubbed his face with his hands.
The phone goes to Bağlarbaşı at 22.19; your car is there at 22.14. The 23.41 message comes from that cell.
Cem Akbulut — third interview

Halil Bey. I’d been following Defne for three days. ‘Where she goes, who she meets, tell me,’ he said. When I took the phone I saw a number on it; a message saying ‘test’ had come in. I texted the number to Halil Bey. He did the rest.

Statement of the person reported missing.

Halil Bey. Nobody knew the number. ‘I know you met Onur. I know where your phone is, too,’ he said. He didn’t threaten me. He didn’t need to. I left the guesthouse and set off for Onur’s; there was someone behind me. I didn’t call Onur. I spent the night in a hotel I didn’t know.
The call to your new line at 23.26?
I left the originals with a solicitor I trust on Friday morning. Onur has a copy. I didn’t come forward because I didn’t know who to trust. I still don’t.
Where are the documents now?
I’m not ready to talk about that yet.
I was testing whether the new line worked. I sent it to the old phone, read it, then left the phone. That’s where they found the number, isn’t it?
Answered her own question; closed her eyes.
The “test” message at 21.40?
I didn’t send it. That phone wasn’t with me; I left it on the seafront and never touched it again. A message like that to Buse… I don’t write like that. Buse knows.
There was a long silence. Then she slowly raised her head.
Why did you send your sister a message at 23.41?

Because I wanted it found. I left my ID and wallet at home, so I’d look lost, not run off. I took the lock off too, so whoever found it would see straight away whose it was. I wanted nobody looking for me for a while, so I could get the documents somewhere safe and then decide what to do. It wasn’t running from Halil Bey… it was moving before he did.
Clasped her hands together; her voice was level.
Why did you leave your phone on the seafront?
“Because I wanted it found.”
Defne Yalın — interview

The sealed envelope handed over by Onur Taşkın was opened with a written record:

· Copies of 14 progress payment claims issued in the names of Doğa Altyapı, Karen İnşaat and Mevsim Yapı. The documents of three separate companies have the same zoning parcel, the same work item and the same quantities.
· The payment instructions for these claims; on every one, the approval signature: Halil Ertan.
· Trade registry summaries for the three companies; all three have an authorised officer at the same address.
· A handwritten note: “The originals aren’t with me. This copy is in case I can’t be reached.” — D.Y.
ENVELOPE CONTENTS — HANDOVER RECORD

Cem Akbulut was held solely responsible. Halil Ertan issued a statement saying ‘The company is not responsible for the personal conduct of its staff’; the progress payment file did not reach anyone’s desk for some time.

An investigation was opened into Halil Ertan on suspicion of false progress payments and of having an employee followed. Cem Akbulut repeated in his written statement that he had sent the 23.41 message. The envelope held by Onur Taşkın entered the file as evidence.

Onur Taşkın was thought to have been with Defne to watch over her; his phones were examined and nothing turned up. When Defne learned that the person she trusted most was being treated as a suspect, she broke off the interview.
Who was behind the following remained an open question in the file. When Defne Yalın saw the question had gone unanswered, she moved.

The file was handled as an abduction; Onur Taşkın was taken into custody for having received an envelope in the café. When Defne Yalın came forward through her solicitor, Onur was released; Halil Ertan’s name did not come up at all in the first weeks.
The file was closed as ‘undetermined’. Defne Yalın kept putting off coming forward; the documents waited in a solicitor’s safe.
MISSING PERSON UPDATE — Defne Yalın has been confirmed alive and well through an interview with her. At Yalın’s request, her location has not been added to the file.

Statement of Defne Yalın’s manager.
That is an internal company matter. If necessary, our legal department will reply in writing.
Thursday, at the end of the working day. She left a little after six. She said good evening, as always.
Straightened his wristwatch; he did not look away as he spoke.
When did you last see Defne?
I left the office and went home. I had dinner with my family. I went to bed early.
Where were you on Thursday evening?
No. Why would I? When she didn’t come in the next day I called once; it was off.
Gave the answer before the question was finished.
Did you call Defne that night?
Defne had private matters lately. She was distracted. Sometimes she stayed late in the evenings; I asked, and she said ‘a backlog’. I didn’t press her. I don’t get into people’s private lives.
Stressed the word ‘private’ twice.
Have you noticed any change at work recently?
“Defne had private matters lately.”
Halil Ertan — interview
Interview held after the building camera.

…Yes. Her phone wasn’t off, but she wasn’t answering. I’d seen the archive notifications; I wanted to talk. Company documents can’t be in an employee’s home. She didn’t open the door; I left. I said I was at home because I knew where this question would take you.
Never raised his voice; it was as if he had built his sentences in advance.
Archive notifications are routine. Things a manager has to see.
On Thursday night at 22.38 you were at Defne’s door.
Approval is my job. The subcontractor prepares the content of the documents; the site checks it. I won’t discuss this without our legal department.
His face closed.
The progress payment claims of three subcontractor firms contain the same work items; the approvals are yours.
I gave Cem no such instruction. Cem is site staff; paperwork isn’t his job. Ask him yourself why he said that.
Paused for a moment; then gave the answer in a single breath.
Cem Akbulut says he was waiting in Bağlarbaşı for paperwork that night on your instructions.

Statement of the friend who met Defne at the café.
Towards eleven at night a number I didn’t know called. I didn’t answer; I don’t answer unknown numbers at midnight. It didn’t call again.
Did anyone call you that night?
I can’t say that. I promised.
Yes. She wrote, ‘Let’s have a coffee.’ We just talked. Old times, her work. She was tired, that’s all.
Played with the zip of his coat, then put his hand on the table.
On Thursday evening you met Defne at Rıhtım Kahve.
“We just talked.”
Ordinary things. She said she was fed up with work. She said maybe she’d get out of the city for a while. I said that would be good.

Onur Taşkın — interview
She wasn’t scared. She was determined. Like she’d planned something. She looked at her watch twice; like she had somewhere to be.
Was Defne scared?
Interview held after the café employee’s statement.

…Yes. She left it. ‘If I’m not around for a few days, keep this, don’t give it to anyone, don’t even open it yourself,’ she said. I promised. That’s why I didn’t say. But now… now she’s missing. Here. I didn’t open it, I swear.
Took a long breath. He took the envelope out of his bag and laid it on the table.
The waiter says Defne left you an envelope.

I don’t know. Maybe because I have nothing to do with her work. So nobody would think of me.

Statement of the attendant at the guesthouse in Kuzguncuk.

Her room is right by the door. Around half eleven her phone rang. She talked briefly. Then she came down, white as a sheet. ‘I have to go; I don’t want the money back,’ she said. Out she went. The time? It hadn’t been twenty minutes.
Did anything catch your attention during the night?
I don’t meddle in my guests’ business, dear.

There was. Towards half past ten. A young lady with a backpack and a coat. She paid in advance, two nights. She said she’d bring her ID later; I wrote ‘Deniz Yıldız’ in my book. She gave me a false name, but I don’t forget a face. The lady in the photograph.
Looked at the photograph for a long time, then nodded.
Did a woman come to the guesthouse on Thursday night?
I saw one. A small, old model thing. Not a smartphone, I think.
How many phones did she have?
“She gave me a false name, but I don’t forget a face.”

CELL TOWER RECORD — DEFNE YALIN (OLD LINE)

The cell tower record shows the phone did not stay on the seafront all night: it leaves at 22.03, waits in Bağlarbaşı and returns at 00.08. In the same interval Cem Akbulut’s company car is in the Bağlarbaşı car park; the seafront camera shows a man in a dark coat taking something from the bench and putting it back. The call log reveals the number sent from Cem to Halil and Halil’s 23.26 call, and the statements of Defne and Sevim Ulus show that Defne did not send the message.

The missing person is not always the victim, and the one who lies is not always guilty. Defne staged her own disappearance; Onur kept his word; Cem told half a truth. ‘She disappeared of her own accord’ was right but incomplete: someone turned that plan to his own use with a single message.
Üsküdar, Bağlarbaşı and Kuzguncuk — 9–10 March 2028

Defne Yalın noticed false subcontractor progress payments approved by finance director Halil Ertan and copied them from the archive over three nights. Halil learned of it from the notifications and had site supervisor Cem Akbulut follow Defne. Defne had planned her own disappearance: she opened a new line, left a copy with Onur Taşkın at 20.43, texted ‘test’ from the new line to her old phone at 21.40 and put the phone under the bench on the seafront at 21.51. Cem took the phone at 22.02, passed the number to Halil, sent the message to Buse from Bağlarbaşı at 23.41 and put the phone back on the bench at 00.06. Halil called the new line at 23.26; Defne fled the guesthouse, spent the night in a hotel and got the original documents to a solicitor in the morning.
What was Defne’s first disappearance?

From the statement of Elif Kuzu, who works as a waiter at Rıhtım Kahve:

“I looked after the table by the window. The woman had a backpack; she ordered tea and didn’t drink it. After the man came, they talked in low voices. As the woman got up, she took a brown envelope out of her bag and put it down in front of the man, and said something like ‘If I’m not around, keep it.’ The man put the envelope inside his coat straight away.”

From the photographs shown to her, Elif Kuzu identified the man as Onur Taşkın.
